readings.title: The Virtue of Simplicity
readings.challenge: List the kinds of simplicity Washington asks for (in attitude, work, spending, dress and speech). Then decide what single danger they all guard against.
readings.focus: Humility and thoroughness as the foundation of a growing institution, and plain living as an answer to hostile laws.
readings.context: Booker T. Washington (1856–1915), born into slavery in Virginia, founded Tuskegee Institute in Alabama in 1881 and led it until his death. Character Building (1902) collects the Sunday evening talks he gave to Tuskegee’s students and teachers. William H. Baldwin, Jr., a railroad president, chaired Tuskegee’s board of trustees; John D. Rockefeller, Jr., son of the founder of Standard Oil, visited and spoke at the school in 1901. Students built many of Tuskegee’s buildings themselves, making the bricks and laying them. Collars were then detachable and starched, and a laundered collar was a mark of prosperity. Around 1900 several Southern states, Alabama among them in 1901, passed laws and constitutions that took the vote from Black citizens and enforced segregation.

excerpt.locator: Character Building, complete address “The Virtue of Simplicity”; opens “I hope that you all paid strict attention to what Mr. William H. Baldwin, Jr., who…”; closes “…to be respected and praised and recognized will be respected and praised and recognized.”.

questions.prompt: Washington warns that success “may injure them more than poverty.” Why does he fear success for Tuskegee, and what does he say humility does not mean?
facilitatorNotes: If the school becomes “stuck up,” its supporters will lose confidence, and it depends on their goodwill to grow. Humility keeps the school thorough and worthy of support. But he insists that being humble does not mean being “cringing and unmanly.”

Students may notice that his advice is both a moral principle and a practical strategy for a Black school in the South relying on donors. Discuss whether the two motives strengthen or weaken each other.
evidence: success may injure them more than poverty
I do not mean that it is necessary for us to lose sight of what the world calls manhood and womanhood; that it is necessary to be cringing and unmanly

questions.prompt: What exactly does Washington object to in the poor student with the shining laundered collar? Is his objection fair?
facilitatorNotes: Not the collar itself (“I like to see every collar shine”) but the pretence: a student whose tuition is paid by others shows the world a prosperity he does not have. He would rather the money went toward tuition, and the student learned to launder his own collar. “Get the man first.”
Some readers find the example sensible and funny; others think it intrudes on a young man’s small dignity. The text gives his reasons fully, so students can weigh them.
evidence: It is much better for a young man to learn to launder his collars himself, than to pretend to the world that he is what he is not.
I do not, however, want you to get the idea that collars make the man.
I should like to have you pay that money for a part of your tuition

questions.prompt: Washington ends by moving from simple words to the laws some states were passing. How does he connect plain living with the struggle against those laws, and are you persuaded?
facilitatorNotes: He urges one-syllable words and praises Rockefeller’s plain speech, then claims that no law or power “can neutralize the influence of a high, pure, simple and useful life,” and that no one can “permanently hold back” a people who gain real strength.

His answer to injustice is character and achievement rather than protest. Some readers find that hopeful and dignified; others ask whether personal virtue can answer laws that took away the vote. Both positions can cite the closing paragraphs.
evidence: If you can get a word with one syllable that will express your meaning, use it in preference to one of two syllables.
there is no power on earth, that can neutralize the influence of a high, pure, simple and useful life
No one can in any way permanently hold back a race of people

readings.title: Have You Done Your Best?
readings.challenge: Count the questions Washington asks and sort them by area of school life. Then decide which reason for doing your best he leans on most.
readings.focus: A midyear self-examination built from questions, and two different reasons for effort.
readings.context: Booker T. Washington (1856–1915), born into slavery in Virginia, founded Tuskegee Institute in Alabama in 1881 and led it until his death. Character Building (1902) collects the Sunday evening talks he gave to Tuskegee’s students and teachers. He gave this talk at the middle of the school year. Tuskegee students took academic classes and also trained in farming, building trades, sewing and cooking, called “industrial work”; many paid their way partly by labour, and the school depended on donors. Washington made the daily use of the toothbrush a school rule.
readings.contentNote: Washington assumes that some students arrived with habits of lying or stealing.

excerpt.locator: Character Building, complete address “Have You Done Your Best?”; opens “[This talk was given at the middle of the school year.]”; closes “…are preparing yourselves to do what this institution and the country expect you to do.”.

questions.prompt: Washington asks students to imagine answering “by their fireside,” in front of parents, friends, teachers and donors. Why frame self-examination this way rather than as a private question?
facilitatorNotes: Imagining these people makes the students’ effort a matter of honesty toward those who “struggled,” “sacrificed” and “toiled for years, in ways you do not know of.” Wasted time becomes a kind of broken trust, not only a personal loss.
Some readers find the appeal to family sacrifice moving; others find it a heavy use of guilt. Both can cite the opening paragraphs.
evidence: suppose you were to-night sitting down by your parents' side, by their fireside
who have struggled, who have sacrificed, who have toiled for years, in ways you do not know of

questions.prompt: Why does Washington spend a whole paragraph on the toothbrush and room inspections? What does “in the dark, as well as in the light” mean?
facilitatorNotes: Small, private habits test whether a person acts from conscience or only for inspection. Using the toothbrush “in the dark” means doing right when no one checks, which is the same honesty he asks for in lessons and work.
Students may find the example comic, but it is deliberate: Washington treats cleanliness and order as part of character. Ask whether a rule kept only for inspection counts as honesty.
evidence: Have you used it in the dark, as well as in the light?
even if your room was not going to be inspected on a certain day

questions.prompt: Washington says both that dishonest effort “does not pay” and that without honest effort you cannot “be yourself in the sight of God.” Are these the same reason? Which does the talk rely on more?
facilitatorNotes: One reason is practical, the other moral and religious. The close leans on the practical (“it doesn’t pay”), but much of the talk appeals to conscience and to the people the student owes. His repeated “It isn’t too late” keeps either motive hopeful.
Some readers think the two reasons support each other; others think that rewarding honesty with success weakens it as a virtue. Either view is defensible from the text.
evidence: it doesn't pay any individual to do any less than his very best
that you could not be yourself in the sight of God

readings.title: European Impressions
readings.challenge: Sort Washington’s observations into lessons he wants his listeners to learn and points on which he says they are already ahead. Then find the one sentence aimed at the whole South.
readings.focus: A traveller’s report used as an argument for practical education and as an indirect criticism of lawlessness at home.
readings.context: Booker T. Washington (1856–1915), born into slavery in Virginia, founded Tuskegee Institute in Alabama in 1881 and led it until his death. Character Building (1902) collects the Sunday evening talks he gave to Tuskegee’s students and teachers. In 1899 friends paid for Washington and his wife, the educator Margaret Murray Washington, to rest in Europe. Swanley, in Kent, had an agricultural college for women. Holstein cattle are a dairy breed; dykes are banks built to hold back the sea. Toussaint Louverture (about 1743–1803), leader of the Haitian Revolution, died a prisoner in France. Camp-meetings were outdoor religious gatherings.
readings.contentNote: A European’s remark refers to lynching in the American South.

excerpt.locator: Character Building, complete address “European Impressions”; opens “Some people here in America think that some of us make too much ado over the matter of…”; closes “…His parting word to me was, "The United States is good enough for me in the future."”.

questions.prompt: Washington begins with the women at Swanley studying chemistry and spreading manure. What criticism is he answering, and why is this example well chosen?
facilitatorNotes: Some Americans thought Tuskegee made “too much ado” about industrial training. He shows educated European women, “graduates from high schools and colleges,” choosing practical agriculture, so such training cannot be called a mark of inferiority.
His phrase “races that are years ahead of us” reflects his belief in gradual racial progress; students may question that framework while granting the force of the example.
evidence: Some people here in America think that some of us make too much ado over the matter of industrial training for the Negro.
intelligent, cultivated women, who were most of them graduates from high schools and colleges

questions.prompt: What should Southern Black farmers learn from the Dutch, and on what points does Washington say his own people are ahead?
facilitatorNotes: He recommends intensive farming of a few acres instead of “fifty acres poorly tilled,” fine dairying, windmills, and college training for farmers. But in “grace, beauty, and carriage,” in public manners and in “all that marks a lady or gentleman,” he says his people do not suffer by comparison.
Balancing advice with praise keeps the talk from sounding like a lecture on inferiority; some readers also hear him answering white Americans’ stereotypes.
evidence: how to make a living from a small plot of ground well cultivated, instead of from forty or fifty acres poorly tilled
in all that marks a lady or gentleman, our people in the South do not suffer at all by the comparison

questions.prompt: “No law; they kill.” How does Washington use a European’s remark to criticise the South, and how direct is he?
facilitatorNotes: He says respect for law is “the great lesson which the entire South must learn,” and lets a foreigner’s shrug name the violence of lynching. He ends with a prayer rather than an accusation.
Readers may find the indirection wise for a Black leader speaking in Alabama in 1902, or too cautious. Notice that the lesson is addressed to “the entire South,” white as well as Black.
evidence: This is the great lesson which the entire South must learn
No law; they kill.
I pray God that no part of our country may much longer have such a reputation as that in any part of the world.

readings.title: What Will Pay
readings.challenge: Test each piece of Washington’s evidence: who says it, how he knows it, and whether it would convince a doubter.
readings.focus: An argument for honesty in the practical language of profit, ending in a larger question.
readings.context: Booker T. Washington (1856–1915), born into slavery in Virginia, founded Tuskegee Institute in Alabama in 1881 and led it until his death. Character Building (1902) collects the Sunday evening talks he gave to Tuskegee’s students and teachers. The Panic of 1857 was a financial crisis in which many American banks failed. Dr. John Hall was a famous New York preacher. A penitentiary is a prison.

excerpt.locator: Character Building, complete address “What Will Pay”; opens “I wish to talk with you for a few minutes upon a subject that is much discussed,…”; closes “…over and over again: "Will it pay me in this world? Will it pay me in the world to come?"”.

questions.prompt: Does Washington argue that honesty is right or that honesty is profitable? Look at how the talk begins and how it ends.
facilitatorNotes: He adopts his listeners’ own question, “What will pay?”, and answers in its terms: dishonesty never pays in business, work or school. But the businessmen’s answer is given “to say nothing of the future life or of doing right for right’s sake,” and the last question adds “the world to come.”
The practical argument opens the door to the moral one. Students may ask whether honesty would still be right if it did not pay.
evidence: nothing short of downright honesty and fair dealing ever paid in any business
to say nothing of the future life or of doing right for right's sake
Will it pay me in this world? Will it pay me in the world to come?

questions.prompt: Why does Washington tell about students who give “half a dozen excuses” for wanting to go home?
facilitatorNotes: It brings the lesson from banks to his listeners’ own lives: honesty means stating “the exact reason” and sticking to it. A student who changes stories reveals that none is true.
Some readers may sympathise with the homesick student; Washington’s point is not that wanting to go home is wrong but that disguising the reason is.
evidence: In some cases I have had students give me half a dozen excuses in little more than the same number of minutes.
The proper thing for students to do, when they wish to go home, is to state the exact reason, and then stick to it.

questions.prompt: How strong is Washington’s evidence? Consider the forty businessmen, the banker William Taylor and Dr. John Hall.
facilitatorNotes: The businessmen are successful men describing their own honesty, so they may not be impartial witnesses; Washington recalls the Taylor story with hedges (“I think it was 1857,” “I believe”). The stories illustrate that reputation is a kind of capital (money flowed into an honest bank during a panic) rather than proving that honesty always wins.
Students might argue that anecdotes are enough for a Sunday talk meant to inspire, or that dishonest people sometimes prosper. “Character is a power” is the claim the stories serve.
evidence: Every one of the forty answered, without hesitation
I think it was 1857
money had been added to the deposits of his bank that day instead of being withdrawn
Character is a power.

readings.title: Some Lessons of the Hour
readings.challenge: Make a list of the lessons Washington wants students to take from the year, then look for the one idea that he says all of them serve.
readings.focus: Washington argues that education aims at goodness, usefulness and power, and that honesty covers time and effort as well as property.
readings.context: Booker T. Washington (1856–1915), born into slavery in Virginia, founded Tuskegee Institute in Alabama in 1881 and led it until his death. Character Building (1902) collects the Sunday evening talks he gave to Tuskegee’s students and teachers. He gave this talk at the start of a school year. Prince Henry of Prussia, the German emperor’s brother, toured the United States in 1902, and Theodore Roosevelt was president from 1901 to 1909.
readings.contentNote: Washington tells his Black students that dishonesty with property is “one of our worst sins,” a generalization that echoes a racist stereotype of his time.

excerpt.locator: Character Building, complete address “Some Lessons of the Hour”; opens “This evening I am going to remind you of a few things which you should get out of the…”; closes “…you will find that it has been worth your while to have spent your time here.”.

questions.prompt: Washington says books, tools and industries are “but the means.” Means to what? How does that claim fit a school famous for teaching trades?
facilitatorNotes: The end is to make a person “good,” “useful” and “powerful,” so that he can have “a helpful influence upon his fellows.” Even at an industrial school, skill is valued for the character and service it makes possible.
Some readers find this a high view of trade education; others ask whether “power” fits with the rest of his advice to be polite and patient.
evidence: Books, tools, and industries are but the means to fit you for something that is higher and better.
The end of all education, whether of head or hand or heart, is to make an individual good, to make him useful, to make him powerful

questions.prompt: What is Washington’s test of “a true lady or gentleman”? Why does the quotation about meeting a prince and a poor man fit that test so well?
facilitatorNotes: The test is how a person treats someone “considered beneath” him, the poor or the ignorant. The quoted man is at ease with a prince and also puts a poor man at ease, so his manners do not depend on rank.
Notice “white or black” in the next paragraph: politeness is to cross the colour line in both directions. Students can discuss whether manners can really ignore rank in a society built on it.
evidence: The test of a true lady or gentleman comes when that individual is brought in contact with some one who is considered beneath her or him
can meet a poor man without embarrassing the poor man
Learn to speak kindly to every individual, white or black.

questions.prompt: How does Washington widen the meaning of honesty? Do you agree that coming to work early is a kind of honesty?
facilitatorNotes: He says a person can be dishonest by taking “time or energy that belongs to someone else.” The worker who asks how little he can do is cheating his employer, while the one who arrives early and asks to stay longer is honest in this larger sense.
Some students will call this generosity or ambition rather than honesty, since the extra time is not owed. Washington wants students to be “above the average man,” not merely honest.
evidence: It is possible for a person to be dishonest by taking time or energy that belongs to someone else, just as much as tangible property.
Put your whole souls into whatever you attempt to do. That is honesty.

questions.prompt: Washington praises President Roosevelt because he “did not know when to lie.” What is surprising about this praise, and what does it suggest about his idea of courage?
facilitatorNotes: The writer he quotes presents not knowing when to lie as a “fault,” as if a politician should deceive; Washington turns it into the highest compliment. Courage here means telling the truth when it may make you “unpopular” or cost you “something that you count dear.”

His claim that honesty put Roosevelt “at the head of the nation” is hopeful; students may question whether truth-telling is always rewarded. Ask what it might have cost Washington himself to speak the full truth to his audiences.
evidence: one of the President's greatest faults was that he did not know when to lie
it may deprive you of something that you count dear

readings.title: Your Part in the Negro Conference
readings.challenge: Notice what Washington asks of the students, and also what he expects them to receive from the visitors.
readings.focus: A school opens its doors to farm families and visiting educators, and Washington asks students to see hospitality as part of their education.
readings.context: Booker T. Washington (1856–1915), born into slavery in Virginia, founded Tuskegee Institute in Alabama in 1881 and led it until his death. Character Building (1902) collects the Sunday evening talks he gave to Tuskegee’s students and teachers. Each year Tuskegee held a Negro Conference, at which hundreds of Black farmers and their families from the surrounding country came to describe their conditions and hear advice, followed by a Workers’ Conference for teachers from other schools. College extension work means a college teaching people outside its own students, for example through lectures in farming districts.

excerpt.locator: Character Building, complete address “Your Part in the Negro Conference”; opens “For eight or nine years, now, it has been our custom to hold here what is known as the…”; closes “…something that will make their lives happier, brighter, stronger and more useful.”.

questions.prompt: How did the Conference begin, and what does Washington mean by calling it the farmers’ “one day of schooling in the whole year”?
facilitatorNotes: It began with a few invited men and women who described their condition and suggested how the school, and they themselves, could help. For many farmers it is the one day of the year given to their own improvement, so the students’ welcome matters a great deal.
The visitors speak first: the conference starts by listening rather than lecturing. Ask why that order might matter.
evidence: to tell us in a very plain and straightforward manner something about their material, moral and religious condition
We sometimes speak of it as their one day of schooling in the whole year

questions.prompt: Washington says “not every person who cannot read and write is ignorant.” Why do you think he says this to students who are proud of their schooling?
facilitatorNotes: Students might look down on unlettered farmers, perhaps their own parents. He insists that learning runs both ways: he has “learned much” from people who cannot write a word.
The point fits his other talks, which warn educated young people against contempt for home. Students can name kinds of knowledge that books do not give.
evidence: not every person who cannot read and write is ignorant
we can learn something from them notwithstanding, while they are here, and they can learn something from us

questions.prompt: What does Washington ask students to do for the visitors, and what does he promise they will gain?
facilitatorNotes: They should guide farmers through the shops and fields, give up their rooms if needed, and be attentive to visiting educators. In return they gain practical knowledge to carry home and the happiness of serving: “To get the greatest happiness out of life is to make somebody else happy.”

He also wants them to start “local conferences” across the South, so the school’s method spreads. Some readers notice he says that no student ever refused to give up a room, a way of making refusal hard.
evidence: I do not think that in the history of the school a student was ever asked to give up his room to any of these people that he did not gladly and freely do so
To get the greatest happiness out of life is to make somebody else happy.

questions.prompt: How does Washington define a gentleman here? Is it a definition about class, about manners, or about something else?
facilitatorNotes: “A generous person; one who has learned to be kind,” who thinks of “the happiness and welfare of others” first. He applies it to “each boy and each girl,” so it is a matter of character open to anyone, not birth or money.
The old word usually named a social rank; Washington redefines it for students who were often the children of formerly enslaved people. Students can compare it with how the word is used today.
evidence: A gentleman means simply this: a generous person; one who has learned to be kind
I want each boy and each girl who belongs to this institution to be deep down in his or her heart a gentleman or a lady.

readings.title: What Is to Be Our Future?
readings.challenge: Follow how a donor’s question about one school becomes a question about a whole people. Then test the final sentence against the example that comes just before it.
readings.focus: Washington’s case that improvement and visible achievement, not argument, will overcome prejudice.
readings.context: Booker T. Washington (1856–1915), born into slavery in Virginia, founded Tuskegee Institute in Alabama in 1881 and led it until his death. Character Building (1902) collects the Sunday evening talks he gave to Tuskegee’s students and teachers. Tuskegee depended on gifts from wealthy white donors in the North and South. When Washington gave this talk, Black Southerners were losing the vote under new state laws, and segregation was spreading. A will is a document that leaves property after death; Clinton, Iowa, is a small Midwestern city.
readings.contentNote: Washington describes two Black businessmen as “specimens of our race” and treats rights as something Black Americans must earn by proving themselves to white observers.

excerpt.locator: Character Building, complete address “What Is to Be Our Future?”; opens “Last Thursday afternoon I received a telegram from a gentleman stopping for a time in a…”; closes “…you will find that just in proportion as we do this, we are going to get all we deserve.”.

questions.prompt: The donor asks what the future of Tuskegee will be. Why does Washington say the outside world is “sure,” and what question does he think matters more?
facilitatorNotes: He is confident that money will come if the school deserves it. The real question is whether students and teachers will be “worthy of that support,” so he moves responsibility from the donors to his listeners.
Some readers find this empowering; others notice how much the school’s fate still depends on pleasing wealthy outsiders.
evidence: so far as the outside world is concerned, Tuskegee is sure
Are we going to be worthy of that support?

questions.prompt: What is the difference between doing work and improving it? Why does Washington insist that an institution cannot “stand still”?
facilitatorNotes: Many people will sweep a room or plough a field; few find better ways to do it. He asks students to “put brains into our work,” improving every year, because a school, like a person, grows either stronger or weaker.
Students can test the claim against their own school or teams. Is standing still really impossible?
evidence: the difficulty comes in finding persons who make improvements in the manner of sweeping rooms
It is absolutely impossible for an institution to stand still

questions.prompt: Washington concludes: “We cannot talk our way into our rights.” How does the Clinton, Iowa, story support this, and what does his aside about the town’s few Black residents reveal?
facilitatorNotes: Two well-run restaurants won the trust of white townspeople, which supports his claim that visible achievement changes opinion. But he admits that the good opinion may come partly from there being few Black people in the town, which weakens the example.

In 1903 W. E. B. Du Bois criticized Washington for asking Black Americans to earn rights that were already theirs. Students may agree with Washington’s strategy, with Du Bois, or see value in both; ask them to point to sentences.
evidence: The trouble was that there were not many coloured people there.
We cannot talk our way into our rights; we must work our way, think our way, into them.

readings.title: What You Ought to Do
readings.challenge: Trace how the talk moves from a comparison with the human body to hard facts about rural schools, and then to a demand on the listeners.
readings.focus: Washington asks graduates to repay a free education by settling as teachers in the poorest country districts of the South.
readings.context: Booker T. Washington (1856–1915), born into slavery in Virginia, founded Tuskegee Institute in Alabama in 1881 and led it until his death. Character Building (1902) collects the Sunday evening talks he gave to Tuskegee’s students and teachers. Most Black Southerners then lived in the country, many as tenant farmers or sharecroppers on large cotton plantations, often in debt to the landowner. Southern states spent far less on schools for Black children, and many country schools ran only a few months a year. Hampton (where Washington studied), Talladega, Fisk and Atlanta were schools and colleges for Black students; Oberlin College in Ohio, founded in the 1830s, was among the first to admit Black students and women. The “wandering Jew” is a figure from a medieval Christian legend, condemned to wander the earth until the end of time.
readings.contentNote: Washington calls many Black city dwellers “shiftless,” speaks of rural Black communities as “dark communities,” and uses the expression “the wandering Jew,” which comes from an antisemitic legend.

excerpt.locator: Character Building, complete address “What You Ought to Do,” with Washington’s later bracketed note; opens “It is comparatively easy to perform almost any kind of work, but the value of any work is…”; closes “…the South, and in the general condition of the people as described to me then.—B. T. W.]”.

questions.prompt: Washington opens with digestion and with a speaker’s voice reaching the back of a hall. What do these comparisons have in common, and what do they say about the purpose of a school?
facilitatorNotes: Both are about reaching what is far away: food must nourish “the most extreme parts,” and a speaker must be heard by those far off. Schools, likewise, are “of little value” unless their influence reaches people “remote” from education.
The comparisons make the school part of a body, the whole people, rather than a place for the few who attend. Ask whether this makes a school responsible for people who never enter it.
evidence: to make those who are far away from them hear them as well as those who sit near
institutions of this kind are of little value unless they can pave the way to make the results of their work felt among the masses of the people who are especially remote from these institutions

questions.prompt: What facts does Washington give about country schools and farm labour? What does he think causes the poverty he describes?
facilitatorNotes: Schools open four months or less, teachers paid ten to twenty dollars a month, farmers “at the mercy of the landowners.” He says the people work hard but “do not know how to realize on the results of their toil.”

He blames ignorance more than the landowners, though he names them. His harsh word “shiftless” for some city dwellers sits beside praise of the masses’ “thrift and industry”; students can weigh the two.
evidence: in hardly any country district in that state was there a public school which is kept open longer than four months
they are too often at the mercy of the landowners
they do not know how to realize on the results of their toil

questions.prompt: Why does Washington say the students owe a debt, and to whom? Is his argument fair?
facilitatorNotes: Their buildings and teaching are paid for by others, so their education is “a gift from the public.” They owe it “to ourselves, but to our race and our country,” and he adds that it is “a religious debt.”

Some students will find the reasoning convincing; others may ask whether a gift creates a duty, or whether the duty should fall on the states that underfunded the schools. He also promises that the sacrifice will be short and the teachers will be well supported.
evidence: Your education, in a large measure, is a gift from the public
This is a debt that you owe not only to yourselves, but to our race and our country.

questions.prompt: Washington compares rural teachers with the settlers of the West and the founders of Oberlin. What does the comparison suggest about how he wants students to see themselves? What does the closing bracketed note add?
facilitatorNotes: They are to be pioneers, enduring hardship to plant institutions that later generations will take for granted. The advice to stay in one place, not to become “the wandering Jew,” follows from that: a pioneer settles.

The bracketed note, added later, reports some improvement, as if to say the talk worked. Readers may notice that the Western settlers took land from Native peoples, which complicates the heroic comparison; Washington does not consider it.
evidence: This same kind of pioneer work had to be done all over the world before the right kind of civilization was planted.
resolve to plant yourself in one community and stay there

readings.title: Individual Responsibility
readings.challenge: Washington builds this talk on two true stories from the school. Retell each in a sentence, then decide what single habit separates them.
readings.focus: Washington argues that each person is responsible for the outcome of the work that passes through his hands, and that “luck” is often another name for that habit.
readings.context: Booker T. Washington (1856–1915), born into slavery in Virginia, founded Tuskegee Institute in Alabama in 1881 and led it until his death. Character Building (1902) collects the Sunday evening talks he gave to Tuskegee’s students and teachers. A recitation was a class session in which students answered questions on the day’s lesson. Chehaw was the railway junction a few miles from Tuskegee, where trains north and south could be met; Montgomery is the capital of Alabama; Phelps Hall was a building on the campus. An “eye-servant,” from the Bible’s warning against “eyeservice,” is someone who works only while being watched.

excerpt.locator: Character Building, complete address “Individual Responsibility”; opens “I have referred in a general way, before this, when I have been speaking to you, to the…”; closes “…or "lucky?" I think it would be much more suitable to say of him: "He is responsible."”.

questions.prompt: Washington says that failing a recitation is not “nobody's business but my own.” Whom else does it affect, according to him? Do you find the argument convincing?
facilitatorNotes: It lowers the class average and so the teacher’s reputation, and it sets an example: another student reasons that if one boy fails and “still he gets along,” failing once cannot matter. Our actions always “touch” other lives.
Some students will think the teacher argument is weak, since the teacher should not be blamed for lazy pupils, a point Washington himself admits. The example argument is stronger.
evidence: It is nobody's business but my own if I fail in a recitation.
He has failed in class ever so many times, and still he gets along. It can't make much difference if I fail once.

questions.prompt: Retell the story of the note to the barn. Who was to blame? What does Washington say a person should do when a task passes out of his hands?
facilitatorNotes: The note passed from boy to boy, and no one made sure it arrived, so no carriage came and the visitor nearly missed his train. Each could blame the next; that is exactly the problem. Washington says responsibility does not end when you hand a task on: you must impress it on the next person.
He dismisses apologies after the fact: “no amount of saying, ‘I am sorry’ ... will help the matter any.” Students can think of group projects where the same thing happens.
evidence: no one had taken enough interest in the errand to see that whatever business the note referred to received proper attention
do not feel that your responsibility in the matter ends until you have impressed it upon the minds and heart of the person to whom you turn over the further performance of the duty

questions.prompt: The boy who saw smoke at Phelps Hall turned out to be worried for nothing. Why does Washington praise him anyway?
facilitatorNotes: Others would not have noticed, or would have said it was none of their business. He searched the building to the attic because unusual smoke might mean danger. The value lies in the habit of caring, not in this one result.
Washington says the buildings are “safer for his being here.” Ask whether such a habit can be taught, and how.
evidence: still others would have said that it was none of their business anyway, and would have gone along
I shall feel that all of our buildings are safer for his being here

questions.prompt: Washington rejects the word “lucky” for the successful boy and prefers “He is responsible.” What is persuasive about this, and what might it leave out?
facilitatorNotes: He shows the first boy doing more than he is paid for and the second watching the clock, so success follows character. Calling it luck hides the choices that made the difference.

But he assumes the two boys “started out in life equal-handed.” Students may point out that for many people, especially Black workers in the South of his day, prejudice and poverty limited how far effort could carry them. Washington’s answer would be that effort is the part each person controls.
evidence: There is no such nonsense as that.
The second boy was an eye-servant who was afraid that he would do more than he was paid to do
I think it would be much more suitable to say of him: "He is responsible."

readings.title: What Would Father and Mother Say?
readings.challenge: Notice how the talk turns halfway, from what students should avoid to what they should learn. Decide which half Washington thinks matters more.
readings.focus: A test of conduct borrowed from home, and a lesson in practical kindness.
readings.context: Booker T. Washington (1856–1915), born into slavery in Virginia, founded Tuskegee Institute in Alabama in 1881 and led it until his death. Character Building (1902) collects the Sunday evening talks he gave to Tuskegee’s students and teachers. Many Tuskegee students were the first in their families to go away to school, and their parents often struggled to keep them there. The officer of the day enforced rules; students drilled on a parade ground. General Samuel Chapman Armstrong founded Hampton Institute in Virginia, where Washington himself studied. A theological seminary trains ministers.

excerpt.locator: Character Building, complete address “What Would Father and Mother Say?”; opens “I think there is no more important or more critical time in a person's life than when he…”; closes “…about my doing this?" will enable you to answer the question with pride and satisfaction.”.

questions.prompt: Washington offers a test: “What would my father or my mother think of this?” Why does he think it works, and when might it fail?
facilitatorNotes: It reminds students of the people who sacrificed for them and makes every act something they would or would not be willing to report home. He adds that knowledge and skill are worthless without “high, upright character.”
Students may point out that the test assumes wise parents, or that growing up sometimes means disagreeing with one’s family. Washington is speaking to young people far from home for the first time.
evidence: There is no better way to test an act than to ask yourself the question
We can fill your heads with knowledge, and we can train your hands to work with skill, but unless all this training of head and hand is based upon high, upright character

questions.prompt: How does Washington make the story of the mother’s message powerful? Look at its timing and his questions.
facilitatorNotes: The message from a struggling mother arrives after her son “had already disgraced himself” and been sent away. Washington asks “where was that boy?” and answers himself, so the audience feels the gap between the mother’s hopes and the son’s conduct.
His last remark, that the boy was trying to hide his disgrace, shows the father-and-mother test working by its absence.
evidence: Now, when this message was delivered, where was that boy?
He had already disgraced himself, and had been sent away from the institution.
No wonder he was trying to conceal his misconduct and disgrace from her.

questions.prompt: What does Washington call “the greatest lesson of all,” and why does he end with the seminary students who offered to black his boots?
facilitatorNotes: Brotherly love shown in small acts: giving a seat in chapel to a stranger, inviting a new student to share a table. General Armstrong’s unselfishness and the seminary students’ eagerness to serve their guest are his models.

He does not say so, but advanced theology students offering to black a Black visitor’s boots reversed the usual pattern of service in 1902; students may infer why the experience impressed him. The talk ends by tying kindness back to the parents’ approval.
evidence: the greatest lesson of all is the lesson of brotherly love, of usefulness and of charity
they will rise in chapel and give their seats to students who are strangers at the school
they were not above serving me, even to the extent of offering to black my boots

readings.title: Substance vs. Shadow
readings.challenge: Apply the title to each example: name the shadow and the substance in the wedding, the titles and the memorial collection.
readings.focus: Show and reality: a practical argument about education, spending and pride.
readings.context: Booker T. Washington (1856–1915), born into slavery in Virginia, founded Tuskegee Institute in Alabama in 1881 and led it until his death. Character Building (1902) collects the Sunday evening talks he gave to Tuskegee’s students and teachers. Tuskegee combined academic subjects with “industrial education,” training in trades and farming. Osnaburg is a coarse cotton cloth; a Prince Albert is a long frock coat; hacks are hired carriages; to engross a document is to copy it out in large, formal handwriting. The Pilgrims landed at Plymouth, Massachusetts, in 1620.
readings.contentNote: Washington mocks Black Southerners and city-dwellers who spend on show, and the talk includes period assumptions about husbands and wives.

excerpt.locator: Character Building, complete address “Substance vs. Shadow”; opens “You are here for the purpose of getting an education. Now, one of the results of an…”; closes “…of real worth. We want you to teach by word and action simple, right and honest living.”.

questions.prompt: Washington claims that education “increase[s] a person’s wants.” Why does that create a crisis, and what is his solution?
facilitatorNotes: Once educated, a person wants more rooms, better clothes, a collar and tie. The crisis comes if education has not also increased the ability to pay for these things; his solution is industrial education, which builds skill alongside culture.

Notice that he never calls the new wants wrong. Students might decide whether the argument is about limiting wants or about matching them with ability, and whether “shallow culture” is a fair name for learning that does not pay.
evidence: So you see the result of education is to increase a person's wants.
whether his education has increased his ability to supply his wants

questions.prompt: Choose one of the three examples (the wedding, the titles or the memorial collection) and explain what the shadow and the substance are in it. Which example is the most persuasive?
facilitatorNotes: The $150 wedding is show, followed by a rented one-room cabin; the many “doctors, professors, or colonels” are titles without worth; the $6.00 engrossing leaves sixty-five cents for the school. The memorial story is the most exact, because Washington counts the cost.
Some students will find the wedding example unkind or out of date; accept other choices if the shadow and substance are clearly named.
evidence: The engrossed resolutions were the shadow; the sixty-five cents were all that was left of the substance.
how much better it is to get married for four dollars, and to pay as you go

questions.prompt: Washington jokes about “five dollar hats on heads that at most are not worth more than fifty cents.” Is his ridicule fair? Consider why fine clothes and titles might have mattered to Black Americans in 1902.
facilitatorNotes: Washington uses humour to shame his own listeners into thrift. But in the Jim Crow South, white people commonly refused to call Black adults “Mr.” or “Mrs.,” so dress and titles could be claims to the dignity that was being denied.

Washington himself advises, “If you are a mister, encourage the people to call you by that title.” Students may defend the advice as practical or criticize the mockery as echoing white stereotypes; both readings are defensible.
evidence: wearing five dollar hats on heads that at most are not worth more than fifty cents
If you are a mister, encourage the people to call you by that title.

readings.title: Character as Shown in Dress
readings.challenge: Test Washington’s opening claim against the rest of the talk. Separate his economic arguments from his judgments about taste.
readings.focus: Dress as a sign of priorities, and a warning against spending on show.
readings.context: Booker T. Washington (1856–1915), born into slavery in Virginia, founded Tuskegee Institute in Alabama in 1881 and led it until his death. Character Building (1902) collects the Sunday evening talks he gave to Tuskegee’s students and teachers. A fop is a man vain about his clothes; kid gloves are made of fine thin leather. Sixth Avenue in New York and Cambridge Street in Boston ran near the Black neighbourhoods of those cities. Twenty dollars a month was a low wage. Washington’s audience included young women and men, and his advice often addresses them separately.
readings.contentNote: Washington criticises students who lighten their skin with powder and judges young women’s appearance by what men will “respect,” in the attitudes of his time.

excerpt.locator: Character Building, complete address “Character as Shown in Dress”; opens “It is surprising how much we can tell about a person's character by his dress. I think it…”; closes “…your education, but now is the only time that you have in which to secure the education.”.

questions.prompt: Washington opens by saying “we can tell about a person’s character by his dress.” Does the rest of the talk support that claim, or limit it?
facilitatorNotes: He shows dress revealing priorities: the person who goes in rags all week to be showy on Sunday, or spends a month’s wages on gloves and jewellery. But he ends by saying that if students “get something into your head,” dress “will adjust” itself; dress follows character, it does not make it.
Students may question judging anyone by clothes, especially the poor. Washington’s own advice, “Dress in the way that your pocket will allow,” partly answers that objection.
evidence: It is surprising how much we can tell about a person's character by his dress.
Dress in the way that your pocket will allow.
Only get something into your head, and then you will find that these matters of dress will adjust themselves.

questions.prompt: What economic argument lies under Washington’s jokes about fops and brass jewellery?
facilitatorNotes: Money spent on display is money not saved for land, homes or education: a man earning “twenty dollars a month” in kid gloves, or jewellery bought by the piece that wholesales “a bushel” for a few dollars. Multiplied across a whole people, he says, it is “thousands of dollars every year.”
Some readers find the thrift sensible and the comedy (brass you can “almost smell”) effective; others think he polices the small pleasures of poor people. Both readings use his examples.
evidence: who perhaps earn about twenty dollars a month, standing on the street corners with kid gloves on
jewellery that you actually can get for six dollars and seven dollars a bushel at wholesale
Our people spend thousands of dollars every year for this cheap jewellery.

questions.prompt: In the shoes and face-powder passages, what does Washington say people are trying to disguise, and what does he value instead?
facilitatorNotes: They squeeze into small shoes to seem to have small feet, and some powder their faces to “improve our colour,” that is, to look lighter. He answers that “it is just as honourable to have a large foot as a small one” and that there is “no use” in changing one’s colour: nothing about their bodies needs hiding.

His rejection of skin-lightening resists a prejudice that valued lighter skin. Yet he frames the advice in terms of what “any man will” respect in a girl, which many readers today will question. Both points deserve discussion.
evidence: it is just as honourable to have a large foot as a small one
Some of us think we can improve our colour.
There is no use for this.

readings.title: Sing the Old Songs
readings.challenge: Read the quoted songs aloud. For each, compare Washington’s introduction with what the words of the song actually say.
readings.focus: The spirituals as an art of truth and simplicity, and what that art says about slavery.
readings.context: Booker T. Washington (1856–1915), born into slavery in Virginia, founded Tuskegee Institute in Alabama in 1881 and led it until his death. Character Building (1902) collects the Sunday evening talks he gave to Tuskegee’s students and teachers. Here he praises the spirituals that enslaved African Americans created, which Tuskegee students sang in chapel. Hampton Institute in Virginia, where Washington had studied, published a collection of these “plantation melodies.” Prince Henry of Prussia, brother of the German emperor, toured the United States in 1902. Garrison and Phillips were white abolitionists. The songs draw on Bible stories: Daniel saved from the lions, Jonah from the whale, three young men from a furnace, and Jacob’s dream of a ladder to heaven.
readings.contentNote: The songs are printed in the dialect spelling used by collectors of the period. One recalls a boy about to be sold away from his mother.

excerpt.locator: Character Building, complete address “Sing the Old Songs”; opens “There is no part of our chapel exercises that gives me more pleasure than the beautiful…”; closes “…senseless customs, oppressions, will hide their faces forever in blushing shame.”.

questions.prompt: How does Washington explain “A little child shall lead them”? What quality, in his view, has made great leaders?
facilitatorNotes: A child is always its true self, “never appearing big when it is little.” Leaders of every faith and race who stood on that “rock of truth” drew people to them, and his list runs from Luther and Lincoln to Frederick Douglass.
Students might ask whether simplicity is the same thing as truthfulness, and whether the leaders he names were simple men.
evidence: never appearing big when it is little
There is no pretence. There is no mockery.

questions.prompt: Washington calls the spirituals “simple” and “child-like.” Look closely at the Daniel song and the boy’s song. Do they seem simple to you?
facilitatorNotes: “Why can’t He deliber me?” argues from evidence: God freed Daniel, Jonah and the three young men, so why not the enslaved singer? The boy who is to be sold sings “I’m gwine to tell God how-a’ you sarved me,” a promise to testify against those who mistreated him. Both voice protest within faith.
Washington’s “child-like” can mean sincere rather than naive. Some readers think the word undersells the songs’ intelligence and anger; others think it is his highest praise.
evidence: Why can't He deliber me?
I'm gwine to tell God how-a' you sarved me.

questions.prompt: “Why does every attempt at improvement spoil them?” How does Washington move from the songs to a lesson for “an individual or a race”? Is the promise of his final sentence convincing?
facilitatorNotes: The songs are admired because they are real, not imitation; likewise, a person or people who reject “sham” and plant themselves on “the solid granite of nature” will win respect, and prejudice will “hide” its face.
Some readers find the ending inspiring; others find its confidence hard to square with the violence and segregation of 1902. Ask what kind of evidence would test the claim.
evidence: But sham, buffoonery, mere imitation, mere superficiality, never has brought success and never will bring it.
race prejudice, senseless customs, oppressions, will hide their faces forever in blushing shame.

readings.title: Getting Down to Mother Earth
readings.challenge: Track one metaphor (foundation, bed-rock, roots) from the first paragraph to the last, and decide what it allows Washington to argue.
readings.focus: Land ownership and practical skill as the foundation for everything else a people may build.
readings.context: Booker T. Washington (1856–1915), born into slavery in Virginia, founded Tuskegee Institute in Alabama in 1881 and led it until his death. Character Building (1902) collects the Sunday evening talks he gave to Tuskegee’s students and teachers. Most Black Southerners at the time farmed land they did not own, renting it or working for a share of the crop and borrowing against the next harvest, so that many stayed in debt year after year. A note or check that is “honoured” is one a bank or store will accept. Russell H. Conwell was a famous Philadelphia minister; the Independent was a New York weekly magazine.

excerpt.locator: Character Building, complete address “Getting Down to Mother Earth”; opens “One of the highest ambitions of every man leaving Tuskegee Institute should be to help…”; closes “…and have their foundation in Mother Earth. What is true of the tree is true of a race.”.

questions.prompt: Follow the metaphor of foundations through the talk. How does it change from the first paragraph to the last, and what does it let Washington argue?
facilitatorNotes: It begins as a house: without bed-rock, everything is “plaster” and “make-believe.” It ends as a tree whose roots in “clay, and rocks, and sand” feed its blossoms. The first image dismisses show without substance; the second answers critics who say he ignores morals and culture, which grow from economic roots.
Students may test whether a metaphor proves anything, or whether it only makes a case memorable.
evidence: all else is but plaster, but make-believe, but the paper on the walls of a house without framework
You cannot plant a tree in air and have it live.
What is true of the tree is true of a race.

questions.prompt: What makes the story of the Alabama farmer persuasive? What does Washington mean by saying he “seemed to be what the white men about him were”?
facilitatorNotes: For twenty years the farmer looked prosperous on borrowed mules, a borrowed buggy and unpaid clothes; he imitated the appearance of his white neighbours without their ownership. By giving everything back and pulling the plough himself by moonlight, he built a debt-free life and became a bank stockholder.
The story shows independence through ownership, but at enormous cost. Some readers find it inspiring; others notice how much hardship it asks of people denied fair conditions.
evidence: He seemed to be what the white men about him were.
He had resolved to be a man.
by moonlight he pulled a plough which the boy guided

questions.prompt: Washington hopes the race “will remain” agricultural and wants schools to produce “job-makers.” How persuasive do you find his programme?
facilitatorNotes: He argues from numbers (eighty-five per cent farm), from history (nearly every people began on the land) and from independence: ministers who farm can lead rather than cater. He also insists that “nature draws no colour line.”

Some of his contemporaries argued that this programme set Black ambition too low and accepted the loss of political rights. Others saw it as the surest road to independence. Accept either view supported by the text.
evidence: because the race is an agricultural one, and because my hope is that it will remain such
What we should do in all our schools is to turn out fewer job-seekers and more job-makers.
nature draws no colour line

readings.title: Last Words
readings.challenge: Separate Washington’s cautions about going home from his advice about a life’s work, and notice how the talk ends with a claim about what no one can take away.
readings.focus: Washington’s farewell to departing students: return home without pride, settle in the country, and answer prejudice with character.
readings.context: Booker T. Washington (1856–1915), born into slavery in Virginia, founded Tuskegee Institute in Alabama in 1881 and led it until his death. Character Building (1902) collects the Sunday evening talks he gave to Tuskegee’s students and teachers. This talk closes the book and was given at the end of a school year. The Young Men’s Christian Association and the Christian Endeavour Society were church-based youth organizations. Around 1900 most Black Americans lived in the rural South. The “colour line” was the phrase of the time for the legal and social separation of the races.
readings.contentNote: Washington speaks of showing white people that Black people are “not of a belittling race,” language shaped by the prejudice of his time.

excerpt.locator: Character Building, complete address “Last Words”; opens “We have come to the close of another school year. Some of you will go out from among us…”; closes “…about us; and when we possess them, nobody can take them from us by speaking ill of us.”.

questions.prompt: Washington’s first caution is about how students treat their parents. Why does he think this matters so much, and how does the story of the painted house answer it?
facilitatorNotes: He fears education will make students feel “better than the rest of the folks” and ashamed of parents who sacrificed for them; he says it would be better to have no education. The son who repairs and paints his parents’ home shows the opposite: education put to use for the family.
Ask why Washington treats a home repair as “most encouraging.” Students may connect it with their own experience of growing apart from home.
evidence: It would be better for you not to have any education, than for you to go home and feel ashamed of your parents, or not want to help them.
he employed his spare time in fixing up his parents' home

questions.prompt: Why does Washington advise graduates to go to the country rather than the cities? How does he describe the patient work of building a school?
facilitatorNotes: Most Black Southerners live in the country, and the cities already have more help and more temptation. A teacher should begin with a three-month school and add a month at a time, then a proper school-house, while buying land and staying put to win the people’s trust.
His strategy is slow and practical. Students can debate whether advising young people away from the cities limited their opportunities, as his critics said.
evidence: the greater portion, by far, of those who need help live in the country districts
Get them to add one month to three months, and then another month

questions.prompt: What does Washington mean by going out “in a spirit of liberality toward the white people”? How does he guard against this being taken as servility?
facilitatorNotes: Liberality means generosity, helping a white person as gladly as a Black one. He insists it does not mean “lowering your manhood or your dignity”; students are to act “in a manly way.”

Readers differ on whether this generosity toward people who uphold segregation is strength or accommodation. The next sentence, “We want to be larger and broader than the people who would oppress us,” claims moral superiority over the oppressor.
evidence: When I say this I do not mean that you shall go lowering your manhood or your dignity.
We want to be larger and broader than the people who would oppress us on account of our colour.

questions.prompt: The book ends: “when we possess them, nobody can take them from us by speaking ill of us.” What are “them,” and why might Washington choose this as his last word?
facilitatorNotes: They are usefulness, morality, liberality, economy and property: “those qualities which go to make a people and a nation great and strong.” Praise cannot give them and insult cannot remove them, so they are safe from what other people say.

This sums up his strategy: build what cannot be taken away rather than answer words with words. Some readers will note that property and rights were in fact taken from many Black Southerners in these years.
evidence: Nobody can give us those qualities merely by praising us and talking well about us; and when we possess them, nobody can take them from us by speaking ill of us.
